The manipulation of time in the story is very well-balanced and serves its emotional core effectively. In terms of "story time," the actual interaction on the ferry dock takes only a couple of minutes. However, the writer skillfully stretches these brief moments by weaving in rich sensory descriptions (the fog, the sounds of the ferry) and internal reflections. At the same time, the writer uses time compression to condense years of backstory into single sentences—such as summarizing Jonas's childhood habits, or compressing three years of grief and daily routine into the brief description of Ilse pushing Henning's boots aside every morning with her knee. This interplay between a slow, stretched-out present and a tightly compressed past gives the quiet, understated reunion a deep emotional resonance without disrupting the natural flow of the scene.
